units.title: Work types, threads, processes, async tasks and the GIL
outcomes: Choose threads, processes or async tasks from CPU work, I/O waits, shared state and cancellation needs.
Measure CPU-bound thread scaling on default and free-threaded CPython 3.14 builds without assuming their GIL state.
Identify a blocking call that prevents other event-loop tasks from progressing.
units.why: Concurrency overlaps work; it does not automatically make that work parallel. A workload and build-specific experiment is a better design input than a blanket claim about Python threads.

next.note: Protect the state your chosen model shares.

study.title: Concurrency models and Python workload choices
study.locator: Concurrency Models; then Threading vs Multiprocessing, Key Differences and When to Use Threading/Multiprocessing; Asyncio Fundamentals, The Event Loop and Common async/await Mistakes
study.depth: Use the models as a first pass. Check build-specific GIL and process-start claims against the 3.14 references below.

study.title: Free-threaded CPython is a separate build
study.locator: Identifying free-threaded Python; The global interpreter lock in free-threaded Python; Thread safety; Performance characteristics

study.title: Process startup is part of the experiment
study.locator: Contexts and start methods: spawn, fork and forkserver, including the 3.14 default changes and safe importing of the main module

focus: Default CPython 3.14 has a GIL. Pure Python CPU loops do not gain multicore parallelism from its threads; I/O waits and native code that releases the GIL are different cases.

Free-threaded builds can execute Python threads in parallel. Record sys.version, sysconfig.get_config_var('Py_GIL_DISABLED') and sys._is_gil_enabled() after imports; an unsupported extension can re-enable the GIL.
Async tasks share an event-loop thread and yield cooperatively. A synchronous CPU loop or time.sleep inside a task stalls that loop.

Processes isolate state but pay startup and serialization costs. In 3.14 fork is no longer the default anywhere: Linux and other POSIX platforms default to forkserver, while macOS and Windows use spawn. Select and report the context explicitly.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, sum integers with a Python for-loop for four equal jobs of 5,000,000 iterations. Assert each result equals n*(n-1)//2. Compare serial, four threads and four spawned processes on both CPython 3.14 builds. Use one warm-up and five measured trials per mode, include pool startup and save raw times, CPU, full version and GIL state. A reference run on Intel Core i9-12900K gave median seconds serial/threads/processes of 0.304/0.321/0.153 on 3.14.4 default and 0.315/0.088/0.156 on 3.14.6 free-threaded with GIL disabled. These are observations, not required speedups. Also schedule a heartbeat around a synchronous blocking call, then replace it with an awaited nonblocking operation and explain the missing versus advancing heartbeat.
traps: Treating a free-threaded executable name as proof that the GIL stayed disabled after imports.
Replacing the loop with sum(range(n)) and calling it the same pure Python workload, or comparing different total work across worker counts.
Calling asyncio.to_thread a CPU-parallelism guarantee on the default build. It keeps blocking I/O off the loop but does not remove the GIL.

selfTest.q: Which model fits many socket waits with little CPU work?
selfTest.a: Async tasks fit when the client APIs are nonblocking. Threads fit blocking clients. Bound either model's in-flight work.

selfTest.q: Why might processes lose on tiny jobs?
selfTest.a: Startup, serialization and communication can cost more than the CPU work they parallelize.

selfTest.q: Does no GIL mean no need for locks?
selfTest.a: No. Internal container protection does not make a multi-step application invariant atomic.

selfTest.q: Do these two build measurements isolate the cost of removing the GIL?
selfTest.a: No. Patch versions and compilers differ too. Compare scaling within each build; do not attribute every cross-build timing difference to the GIL.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: matched-work concurrency comparisons and an event-loop blocking fault in the bounded worker pipeline.
units.stopWhen: You have correctness-checked raw timings from both builds and can justify a model for CPU work, blocking I/O and cancellation-sensitive work without claiming a universal speedup.

fit.note: Kept the model first pass and the pool's current Python reference; the latter qualifies default-build GIL claims and supplies 3.14 process-start behavior.

units.title: Synchronization primitives and concurrency hazards
outcomes: Protect a compound invariant with a lock and coordinate a bounded queue with condition predicates.
Reproduce a lost update and a deadlock with controlled interleavings, then remove their causes.
Distinguish deadlock, livelock, starvation and lost notification from slow useful work.
units.why: Correct shared-state code needs both safety and progress. A lucky stress run proves neither; force the interleaving that breaks the invariant.

next.note: Apply bounded coordination to admission and draining.

study.title: Locks, permits and progress failures
study.locator: Mutex; Semaphores; Condition Variables; Deadlock; Livelock; Starvation; Lost Signal
study.depth: Read the mechanism and failure examples, not every language implementation. Use Python's Condition contract for the implementation.

study.title: Condition predicates under one lock
study.locator: Condition objects: producer-consumer example, wait, wait_for, notify and notify_all; Semaphore objects

study.title: Design Thread-Safe Blocking Queue
study.locator: Problem Statement, Required Operations, Concurrency Challenges and Approach 1: Single Lock with Conditions
study.depth: Stop before Approach 2. Python locks do not promise the fair-lock starvation guarantee shown in the analysis table.

focus: A lock protects an invariant across all its reads and writes. A semaphore counts admission permits; it does not by itself protect the buffer mutation.
Check the predicate under the condition's lock and wait in a loop. wait releases that lock while sleeping and reacquires it before returning; notify does not release it.
Remove circular lock acquisition with a global lock order. Livelock changes state without useful progress; starvation denies one participant progress while others advance.
Use barriers and events to control test schedules. A timeout detects a stuck test; it does not identify the underlying wait cycle.
units.reproduce: Force two threads to read the same counter before either writes using a Barrier(2) between read and write. After both join, assert 1 instead of the intended 2 on both default and free-threaded builds. Remove that barrier from the critical section, lock the full read-modify-write and assert 2. In a separate test, give two threads opposite first locks, synchronize them at a barrier and use timed second acquisitions to demonstrate the wait cycle without leaving hung threads. Then use one global lock order and assert both finish.
traps: Waiting while holding an unrelated lock needed by the notifier. Condition.wait releases only its own lock.
Putting the test barrier inside the repaired critical section. The first thread then waits for a second thread that cannot enter.
Assuming mutex or condition wakeups are FIFO. Python gives no general starvation-freedom guarantee.

selfTest.q: Why use while rather than if around Condition.wait?
selfTest.a: A wakeup does not reserve the resource. Another participant may consume it before this thread reacquires the lock.

selfTest.q: Does notify preserve a message for a future waiter?
selfTest.a: No. Persistent state is the predicate; check and update it under the same lock used by wait.

selfTest.q: When can empty and full semaphore counts sum to less than capacity?
selfTest.a: After a producer or consumer acquires a permit but before it releases the opposite permit. Reserved in-flight permits are missing from that sum.

selfTest.q: What does a fixed lock order prevent, and what does it not promise?
selfTest.a: It prevents a circular wait among those locks if all paths obey it. It does not guarantee fairness, bounded latency or freedom from other waits.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Design Thread-Safe Blocking Queue
practice.locator: Problem Statement: put, take, offer, poll, peek and size; Approach 1: Single Lock with Conditions
practice.note: Implement the single-lock design in Python. Test capacity one, blocked producer and consumer, FIFO order and unique item delivery with events rather than sleeps. Do not claim Java-style thread interruption or fair-lock guarantees for Python.

units.stopWhen: Your controlled tests expose the lost update and wait cycle, the repairs pass, and the blocking queue preserves its capacity and delivery invariants with multiple producers and consumers.

fit.note: Kept the pool's primitives, hazards and named blocking-queue design. Restricted the Java-oriented solution to one lock and checked its Python semantics against threading.

units.title: Task ownership, cancellation, timeouts and retries
outcomes: Own related tasks with TaskGroup and propagate cancellation after bounded cleanup.
Implement a monotonic end-to-end deadline with classified failures, capped backoff, jitter and a retry budget.
Reject unsafe retries when a timeout leaves a side effect's outcome unknown.
units.why: A task that outlives its caller still consumes capacity. A retry that ignores ownership, deadlines or side effects can turn one transient failure into overload or duplicate work.

next.note: Make retries and cancellation obey the pipeline's admission and drain policy.

study.title: Async task lifecycle first pass
study.locator: Error Handling: TaskGroup for Structured Concurrency (Python 3.11+); Cancellation; Timeout with asyncio.timeout (Python 3.11+)
study.depth: Use the 3.14 reference below for exact failure and cancellation semantics, not older gather-based ownership patterns.

study.title: CPython 3.14 task ownership and deadlines
study.locator: Task cancellation; Task groups and version-change notes; Timeouts: timeout and timeout_at; Running in threads: to_thread

study.title: Retries are additional load
study.locator: Timeouts; Retries and backoff; Jitter
study.depth: The five-layer example's 243 is 3^5 total attempts. Its phrase 'three retries' is inconsistent with that arithmetic; four attempts per layer would give 4^5 = 1024.

focus: TaskGroup awaits owned children on exit. A non-cancellation child failure cancels siblings and groups ordinary errors; one child's CancelledError alone does not fail the group. Clean up in finally and normally re-raise cancellation.

TaskGroup and timeout arrived in 3.11. In 3.13 TaskGroup improved simultaneous cancellation/count handling and closes coroutines submitted while inactive; in 3.14 create_task forwards all kwargs, including eager_start. Do not depend on accidental task-start ordering.

Set one deadline with loop.time() and timeout_at. Queue waits, attempts and backoff spend the same budget. Catch TimeoutError outside the timeout context; cancellation is cooperative, not a hard real-time stop.

Retry only classified transient failures and idempotent operations. Pick one retry owner, cap total attempts and aggregate retry load, and inject clock, random and sleep functions for deterministic policy tests.
units.reproduce: Build an event-gated TaskGroup: one child waits indefinitely with a finally marker, another waits for it to start then raises ValueError. Assert the sibling is cancelled, cleanup ran and except* ValueError receives the failure. Separately assert a child raising CancelledError leaves a successful sibling intact, and an expired timeout around an await becomes TimeoutError outside the context. Add a fake dependency that fails twice then succeeds: three total attempts and full-jitter delays in [0, min(cap, base*2**k)]. Inject random and sleep to check the bounds without wall-clock assertions. Test permanent failure, exhausted budget, expired deadline and cancellation during backoff with no later attempt.
traps: Catching BaseException in a retry loop and thereby retrying CancelledError. Cancellation is not a transient dependency failure.
Giving every attempt a fresh end-to-end timeout. This silently lets retries exceed the caller's deadline.
Assuming cancellation of a to_thread await stops an already-running thread or rolls back a remote side effect. Use cooperative worker stop signals and an explicit unknown-outcome policy.

selfTest.q: What differs between TaskGroup and gather on an ordinary child failure?
selfTest.a: TaskGroup cancels and awaits siblings before reporting grouped errors. Default gather propagates the first error without automatically cancelling its other awaitables.

selfTest.q: Where do you catch asyncio.timeout's TimeoutError?
selfTest.a: Outside its async with block. Inside, expiry is delivered through cancellation of the current task.

selfTest.q: Three total attempts at each of five retrying layers yield what worst-case leaf load?
selfTest.a: 3^5 = 243 leaf attempts for one original request. Three retries plus the initial attempt would instead yield 4^5 = 1024.

selfTest.q: Does a timed-out write prove the server did not commit it?
selfTest.a: No. Its outcome may be unknown. Retry only with a valid idempotency contract or reconcile the result first.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: TaskGroup-owned workers, request deadlines, classified retry budgets, jitter and cancellation cleanup against a fault-injected dependency.
units.stopWhen: Your tests show no child left running after group exit and no retry after cancellation, permanent failure, exhausted budget or deadline expiry; duplicate delivery has an explicit idempotency policy.

fit.note: Coverage failed for operational retry policy, idempotency and jitter. AWS fills that gap; the pool's Python 3.14 reference supplies current TaskGroup and timeout behavior.

units.title: Backpressure, load shedding and graceful shutdown
outcomes: Implement bounded admission with an explicit wait, reject or shed policy under overload.
Account for queued, executing and externally waiting work when setting memory and downstream budgets.
Stop admission, drain accepted work within a deadline and report unfinished work on forced shutdown.
units.why: A queue turns a capacity mismatch into waiting and memory use. Bounding only the queue is not enough if unlimited producers or retry tasks accumulate outside it.

next.note: Expose queue growth, rejection and recovery instead of hiding overload.

study.title: Bounded Buffer
study.locator: Problem Statement; Synchronization Challenges; Solution 2: Semaphore-Based Solution; Solution 3: Monitor-Based Solution (Condition Variables)
study.depth: Skip the Key Insight assertion that empty.count + full.count always equals capacity. It omits permits reserved by in-flight producers and consumers. Do not copy starvation-free claims into Python.

study.title: Bounded queues and drain accounting
study.locator: Queue: maxsize, put, put_nowait, get, task_done, join and shutdown, including immediate shutdown warning and QueueShutDown

study.title: Protect useful capacity during overload
study.locator: The Pitfalls of Queries per Second; Client-Side Throttling; Utilization Signals; Handling Overload Errors, Deciding to Retry; Conclusions
study.depth: Use the local admission and retry-budget principles. Skip Google-specific datacenter balancing and quota infrastructure.

study.title: Deliver termination to the event loop
study.locator: Unix signals: loop.add_signal_handler and loop.remove_signal_handler; main-thread requirement

focus: For W workers taking one item each and queue capacity Q, admitted unfinished items are at most W + Q only if there are no extra prefetches, detached retries or unbounded admission waiters. Bound payload bytes as well as item count.

If arrival rate exceeds service rate, excess work must wait elsewhere or be rejected. A semaphore limits simultaneous work, not starts per second; rate limits and retry budgets protect a different constraint.

Queue.shutdown arrived in 3.13. Graceful shutdown rejects puts, wakes blocked putters and lets existing items drain. Call task_done once per successful get after recording the item's outcome; join tracks unfinished accounting, not business success.

On SIGTERM stop admission first, drain within a monotonic deadline, then cancel and await workers and report unfinished IDs. Immediate shutdown discards queued items; it is an abort policy, not a successful drain.
units.reproduce: Make a two-worker pipeline with Queue(maxsize=2), event-gated consumers and put_nowait admission. Hold two items in workers and two in the queue, assert four admitted unfinished items and reject the fifth with QueueFull. Stop admission using shutdown(), release consumers, await join and assert all four accepted IDs have recorded terminal outcomes. Verify a blocked putter wakes with QueueShutDown. Repeat with shutdown(immediate=True): queued items are discarded and join can return without those items being processed. Add a drain deadline and report abandoned IDs rather than labelling that run successful.
traps: Creating one producer task per arrival before awaiting a bounded put. The queue is bounded but waiting tasks and their payloads are not.
Calling task_done before recording success, failure or abandonment. join can then hide silent loss.
Treating immediate shutdown as proof of completed work. In-flight items still need accounting, and discarded queued items were not processed.

selfTest.q: What changes when lambda exceeds mu for a sustained interval?
selfTest.a: Without rejection, backlog grows roughly at lambda - mu items per second while capacity stays fixed. A bounded queue moves that pressure to admission.

selfTest.q: Is Queue(maxsize=0) a zero-capacity rendezvous?
selfTest.a: No. In asyncio it is unbounded. Use a positive capacity and a separate admission policy.

selfTest.q: Does join prove every accepted item succeeded?
selfTest.a: No. It proves the unfinished-item count reached zero. Your outcome ledger must distinguish success, failure and abandonment.

selfTest.q: Can a concurrency semaphore enforce ten calls per second?
selfTest.a: No. Fast calls can reuse permits many times per second. A time-based rate limiter controls starts; a semaphore controls simultaneous calls.

practice.name: AlgoMaster: Bounded Buffer
practice.locator: Problem Statement, The Rules and The Goal; Solution 3: Monitor-Based Solution (Condition Variables)
practice.note: Solve the bounded producer-consumer contract before reading the solution. Then adapt it to the async mini-project and add overload rejection, outcome accounting and shutdown tests. The semaphore-count shortcut noted above is not an invariant during operations.

units.stopWhen: Your event-gated overload test respects the four-item bound, rejects excess work, drains accepted IDs with explicit outcomes, and distinguishes forced abandonment from successful completion.

fit.note: Coverage failed for load shedding and recovery policy beyond blocking producers. Google SRE adds local overload protection beside the pool's bounded-buffer problem and current queue shutdown API.

units.title: Profiling CPU and memory, and benchmarking honestly
outcomes: Choose sampling, call instrumentation or allocation tracing to test a concrete bottleneck hypothesis.
Distinguish CPU cost, transient allocation peaks and retained Python memory from waiting and process RSS.
Build a correctness-checked benchmark with warm-up, repeated trials and raw results, then justify one optimization and a regime where it does not help.
units.why: Profiles locate expensive work; benchmarks test whether changing it helps. Mixing the two can turn profiler overhead, hidden queueing or a changed workload into an apparent improvement.

next.note: Combine profiles with request-level evidence to separate CPU work from dependency waits.

study.title: High Performance Python, 3rd edition: targeted profiling
study.locator: Chapter 2: Profiling Efficiently (pp. 28-29), Using the cProfile Module (pp. 41-45), Using memory_profiler to Diagnose Memory Usage (pp. 53-60), Introspecting an Existing Process with PySpy (pp. 63-64), Unit Testing During Optimization to Maintain Correctness (pp. 73-76), Strategies to Profile Your Code Successfully (p. 77)
study.depth: Learn tool selection and output interpretation. Do not install every profiler or assume the book's tool versions support both 3.14 builds; execute the stdlib reproduction below.

study.title: Call profiles are not benchmarks
study.locator: Introduction to the profilers; Instant User's Manual: tottime and cumtime; What Is Deterministic Profiling?

study.title: Temporary peaks versus retained allocations
study.locator: Examples: Compute differences; Record the current and peak size of all traced memory blocks; API: get_traced_memory, reset_peak and Snapshot.compare_to

focus: Sampling estimates where observed stacks spend time and can miss short events. Instrumentation records calls but perturbs execution. Choose a supported tool and timer for the hypothesis, not the prettiest report.
cProfile tottime excludes callees; cumtime includes them. Suspended async work and worker processes need separate interpretation; a request's wall time is not its CPU time.

tracemalloc sees traced Python allocations, not all native buffers or RSS. Compare snapshots after the same lifecycle stage for retention; reset the peak for transient allocations and record process memory separately.

Benchmark without profilers under matched input and offered load. Save correctness checks, hardware, Python build, worker count, start method, warm-up, all trials, throughput, latency distribution, rejection rate and queue depth. Include queue wait in end-to-end latency.
units.reproduce: Write sum(list(range(n))) and sum(range(n)) for n=100,000 and check both against n*(n-1)//2. Profile the materialized version with cProfile, then measure traced current and peak memory for each in fresh tracing sessions. The list version should have a larger temporary peak; do not require particular bytes or speedups. Retain 1,000 bytearray(1024) objects, compare snapshots before and after, clear the retaining list, collect garbage and compare again. Then benchmark both sum variants without tracing at small and larger n, with one warm-up and five trials each, saving CPU and full Python version/build with raw times. Explain an optimization's supported workload region rather than extrapolating to a service.
traps: Timing task creation instead of awaiting completion, or hiding admission delay by starting the latency clock only after enqueue.
Calling high RSS a Python-object leak. Allocator retention and native memory can keep RSS high after traced allocations fall.
Reporting the fastest trial, changing total work, or benchmarking with cProfile or tracemalloc enabled.

selfTest.q: What does a high cumtime but low tottime suggest?
selfTest.a: The function's callees account for much of its observed cost. Inspect those callees before rewriting the wrapper.

selfTest.q: Can a snapshot after a function returns reveal its freed temporary list?
selfTest.a: Not as a live allocation. Use peak tracing during the function for temporary memory and snapshots for allocations still retained.

selfTest.q: Why can low CPU usage coexist with high request latency?
selfTest.a: The request may wait in a queue, on a lock, for I/O or for a downstream service. CPU profiles alone do not distinguish all those waits.

selfTest.q: Why keep failures and rejections in a concurrency benchmark?
selfTest.a: A design can appear faster by dropping slow work. Compare completed throughput, end-to-end latency and failure rate at the same offered load.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: CPU and retention diagnosis plus a controlled before/after pipeline benchmark with one justified improvement and one rejected optimization.
units.stopWhen: You can identify the materialization peak and retention site from evidence, preserve the result oracle, and present raw unprofiled trials with a workload-limited conclusion rather than a single best time.

fit.note: Kept the book's bounded profiling selections and used the pool's Python documentation family for current stdlib profiling and allocation APIs; the mini-project supplies service-scale measurement.

units.title: Structured logs, metrics and traces
outcomes: Add structured event logs, low-cardinality counters and latency histograms to a bounded service.
Preserve trace context through async workers and link request logs to the relevant span.
Locate a seeded dependency failure using telemetry while excluding credentials and request payloads.
units.why: A profile explains where code spends resources; telemetry explains which requests and failures are affected. Correlation should make a fault diagnosable without turning every request ID into a metric series.

next.note: Turn the signals into health decisions and recovery instructions.

study.title: Instrument one request, not a whole platform
study.locator: Setup; Traces: Creating spans, Creating nested spans, Get the current span, Set span status, Record exceptions in spans, Change the default propagation format; Metrics: Creating and using synchronous instruments; Logs; Semantic convention stability
study.depth: Use local or in-memory exporters and pin the SDK version. The Logs API/SDK is under development; structured Python logging plus explicit trace/span fields is sufficient. Do not build a Collector deployment.

study.title: Metric attribute sets have a budget
study.locator: Cardinality limits: Configuration, Overflow attribute, Synchronous instrument cardinality limits and Asynchronous instrument cardinality limits
study.depth: Understand limits and overflow, not SDK internals. Keep the application's label space bounded even when an SDK limit exists.

study.title: Minimize sensitive telemetry at the source
study.locator: Your responsibility; Data minimization; Protecting sensitive data; Risk and limitations of hashing for anonymization

focus: Log event name, request ID, trace ID, span ID, outcome class and elapsed time as fields. Allowlist fields before serialization; exception messages and URLs can contain secrets too.

Use counters for completed, failed, rejected and retried work; a histogram for latency; and a gauge for current queue depth. Route templates and bounded error classes are labels; raw paths, user IDs and request IDs are not.

Create child spans while the intended parent context is active. New asyncio tasks copy current context at creation; a long-lived queue worker needs the producer's context carried with each item rather than assumed ambient context.
Trace IDs join per-request evidence but do not describe aggregate health. Sampling may omit a request's trace; keep useful error logs and metrics even when no exported trace is available.
units.reproduce: Instrument a request span with a dependency child span created in an owned async task. Capture spans and structured logs locally, and record a request counter and duration histogram labelled only by route template and outcome. Run 100 distinct request IDs with one seeded dependency failure. Assert child parent IDs and trace IDs agree, logs carry the active span identity, and each metric has only the two expected attribute sets: ok and error. Pass a dummy authorization secret and assert it appears nowhere in exported logs, spans or metrics. Mark the dependency span ERROR and locate that request from the signals, without new print statements.
traps: Putting trace_id or request_id on every metric. Correlation then creates unbounded attribute sets instead of a useful aggregate.
Assuming the context of a task created at startup follows every item it later dequeues. Propagate the item's context explicitly.
Treating hashed user IDs as safe anonymization or recording full exception payloads before redaction. Predictable hashes can be reversed by enumeration.

selfTest.q: Why can two bounded labels still create many metric series?
selfTest.a: Distinct combinations multiply. Budget the full attribute-set space, not each label in isolation.

selfTest.q: Does record_exception automatically express your handled failure policy?
selfTest.a: No. It records an exception event. Set span status deliberately when a handled failure makes the operation unsuccessful.

selfTest.q: Which signal reveals queue pressure without looking up a particular request?
selfTest.a: A queue-depth gauge together with admission rejection, retry and latency metrics. Logs and traces explain individual cases.

selfTest.q: How should a queue worker recover a producer's trace context?
selfTest.a: Carry the context with the item and attach it while processing, detaching in finally. Task-creation context alone is not per-item propagation.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: structured request logs, bounded-label metrics, per-item trace propagation, secret exclusion and diagnosis of a seeded pipeline fault.
units.stopWhen: You can find the seeded failure by request and trace identity, verify parentage and the bounded metric attribute sets, and prove the dummy secret is absent from every exported signal.

fit.note: Kept OpenTelemetry's instrumentation, security and metric-spec pages within the existing resource family. Local exporters and mini-project fault diagnosis reach implement depth without an observability platform.

units.title: Health checks, containers, supervision and runbooks
outcomes: Separate readiness, liveness and startup checks so a dependency outage does not cause a restart storm.
Package a non-root service with pinned inputs, validated runtime configuration, explicit resource limits and a tested termination path.
Write and exercise a runbook for latency, memory growth, worker death, invalid configuration and dependency recovery.
units.why: A running process is not necessarily ready to serve, and restarting it is not always a repair. Health and supervision need distinct contracts backed by an operator's recovery checks.

next.note: Re-measure the service under its actual container limits after a recovery or optimization.

study.title: Three health questions with different actions
study.locator: Liveness probe; Readiness probe; Startup probe
study.depth: Read only the contracts and failure actions. Implement local endpoints; cluster orchestration stays outside this section.

study.title: Containerize a Python service
study.locator: Containerize a Python application: Create the Docker assets, Dockerfile and .dockerignore examples; Run the application
study.depth: Stop before Use containers for Python development. Adapt only the packaging to your service. The sample uses Python 3.12 and an authenticated DHI registry; use an official Python 3.14 image pinned by digest instead, with explicit USER and exec-form CMD as below. No registry login or database is needed.

study.title: Reproducible inputs and a non-root entrypoint
study.locator: Pin base image versions; Exclude with .dockerignore; Dockerfile instructions: CMD, ENV, ENTRYPOINT and USER

study.title: Resource limits and supervision
study.locator: Memory: Limit a container's access to memory, --memory and --memory-swap; CPU: --cpus; then Start containers automatically, Use a restart policy and Restart policy details
study.depth: Use https://docs.docker.com/engine/containers/start-containers-automatically/ for the restart-policy reading. Do not disable the OOM killer or configure privileged scheduling.

study.title: A runbook tests hypotheses and verifies recovery
study.locator: Triage; Examine; Diagnose; Test and Treat; Making Troubleshooting Easier
study.depth: Skip Case Study and Negative Results Are Magic. Use the named method sections to write commands and expected observations for your small service, not an organization-wide incident process.

focus: Readiness controls admission; liveness asks whether restarting can restore progress. Startup checks protect slow initialization. A required dependency may make readiness fail while the process remains live; do not wire every dependency failure to liveness.

Validate typed runtime configuration before becoming ready. Keep secrets outside source, build context and image layers, and redact diagnostics. Pin base-image digests and dependencies, with an explicit update policy.

Use non-root USER and exec-form CMD so the application receives termination signals. Set CPU and memory limits at runtime; CPU quota can throttle, and memory exhaustion can kill the process before it cleans up.

A plain Docker restart policy reacts to process exit, not an unhealthy flag. Choose one supervisor, cap failure restarts where appropriate and record exit/OOM evidence. A runbook names symptom, safe test, expected observation, mitigation, rollback and recovery gate.
units.reproduce: Containerize a small health-enabled version of the pipeline on CPython 3.14 with a pinned base digest, non-root USER and exec-form CMD. Run with --cpus=1 --memory=128m --memory-swap=128m and inspect both configured limits and cgroup values. Validate startup configuration before readiness. Inject a required-dependency outage: readiness fails, liveness stays healthy and recovery restores readiness without a restart. Send SIGTERM with accepted work in flight: readiness drops, new work is rejected and recorded work drains before the stop deadline. In a separate run, force a nonzero process exit and verify a bounded on-failure policy restarts it. Capture exit status and restart count, then follow your runbook to confirm recovery.
traps: Using dependency reachability as liveness. Restarting every replica during a shared outage adds load and loses useful local state.
Deleting a secret in a later Dockerfile layer. The earlier layer still contains it; prevent it from entering the image at all.
Assuming Docker HEALTHCHECK removes traffic or on-failure repairs an unhealthy but running process. Those actions need a separate consumer of the health signal.

selfTest.q: What does a failed readiness probe do in Kubernetes?
selfTest.a: It marks the Pod unready for Service traffic. It does not itself restart the container. Liveness failures trigger restarts after configured tolerances.

selfTest.q: Why distinguish a startup check from liveness?
selfTest.a: A startup probe gates readiness and liveness probing until initialization succeeds, avoiding premature restart decisions.

selfTest.q: Does --cpus=1 reserve a dedicated physical core?
selfTest.a: No. It limits available CPU time through quota. Placement and contention are separate constraints.

selfTest.q: Why check OOMKilled as well as an exit code such as 137?
selfTest.a: An exit code alone does not identify the cause of SIGKILL. Runtime OOM evidence and memory metrics help distinguish limit exhaustion from an external kill.
